# Wheel Alignment Still Feels Off After Getting Alignment

You replaced a control arm and crossmember on your 2007 Nissan Versa, then had an alignment performed at the dealership. Now you feel vibrations while drivingâsomething that never happened beforeâand the printout shows mismatched values between the front left and right wheels. The service adviser claims this is "the best they could get," but looking at the numbers, the symmetry is clearly broken. That discrepancy isn't normal, and it's likely why your car feels unstable.

Wheel alignment involves adjusting three primary angles: camber, caster, and toe. Camber is the inward or outward tilt of the wheel when viewed from the front. Caster affects steering stability and returnability. Toe determines how much the wheels point toward or away from each other when viewed from above. A proper alignment ensures all four wheels are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the road surface, which minimizes uneven tire wear and prevents pulling.

When you replace suspension components like control arms, you're essentially changing the geometry of the wheel assembly. If the replacement part isn't identical in length or angle to the original, or if it's installed incorrectly, the alignment will be off from the start. Even a millimeter difference in control arm length can shift toe or camber significantly. That's why many mechanics recommend doing an alignment immediately after replacing suspension parts.

The vibration you're feeling after the alignment suggests something is still out of balance or misaligned. This could be due to incorrect toe settings, uneven camber, or even a wheel that's not properly seated on the hub. Sometimes, a slight bump in the road can cause the wheels to shift slightly if the suspension isn't fully secured or if the alignment wasn't locked down correctly.

Looking at your printout, if the left and right sides don't match within acceptable tolerance, that's a red flag. Most dealerships aim for symmetry between the two front wheels, especially on toe settings. If one side is set to spec and the other isn't, it could indicate an underlying issue with the suspension geometry or the alignment process itself.

One possible explanation is that the new control arm or crossmember has different mounting points than the original part. Even if the part looks identical, slight manufacturing variances can alter the final alignment angles. In some cases, aftermarket parts aren't as precise as OEM components, which can lead to persistent alignment issues despite best efforts.

Another possibility is that the alignment machine wasn't calibrated correctly or wasn't used properly during the service. Alignment machines rely on precise sensors and reference points; if those aren't accurate, the resulting adjustments will be flawed. Additionally, some shops may not account for wear in other suspension components, like ball joints or bushings, which can affect how the wheel sits once installed.

If you're still experiencing symptoms after the alignment, consider requesting a second opinion from another qualified technician or dealership. Bring your printout and describe exactly what you're feelingâpulling, vibration, noise, etc.âso they can evaluate whether there's an underlying mechanical issue that needs attention beyond just alignment adjustments.

In some cases, replacing multiple suspension components simultaneously may be necessary to restore proper geometry. For example, if only one control arm was replaced while the other is worn, the asymmetry could throw off the entire front-end balance. This is similar to debugging a system where fixing one module doesn't resolve the issue because another part of the architecture is compromised.

Always review alignment printouts carefully, paying attention to symmetry between left and right sides. Small deviations might seem negligible at first glance, but they can accumulate into noticeable handling issues over time. Don't hesitate to ask for clarification on any out-of-spec readings before leaving the service bay. Your safety and driving comfort depend on getting it right the first time.
